title: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
summary: How pretraining loss follows power laws in parameters, tokens and FLOPs, how to split a compute budget (Kaplan vs Chinchilla), and why real models train past compute-optimal.
outcomes: Explain why a power law is a straight line on log-log axes and what its exponent means
Compute training compute with C = 6ND and trade parameters against tokens at a fixed budget
Find the compute-optimal model size from an IsoFLOP curve or the Chinchilla closed form
Explain why Kaplan and Chinchilla disagreed and why GPT-3-era models were undertrained
Decide when to train past compute-optimal because of inference cost, and spot where scaling laws mislead

lessons.title: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space

blocks.md: You know from the pretraining course that a language model is trained to minimize next-token cross-entropy loss, measured in nats per token. A frontier pretraining run costs months of accelerator time, and you usually get one attempt. Before spending that budget you must decide how many parameters the model gets and how many tokens it reads, and you would like to know roughly what loss it will reach.

Trial and error at full scale is unaffordable, and intuition fails because loss improves slowly and unevenly. A **scaling law** is the alternative: an empirical formula, fitted to many cheap small runs, that predicts how loss changes as you scale **model size** $N$ (parameters), **data** $D$ (training tokens) and **compute** $C$ (training FLOPs). If the formula holds over several orders of magnitude, you can extrapolate it to the run you cannot afford to repeat.

Kaplan et al. (2020) trained Transformers from 768 to 1.5 billion non-embedding parameters on WebText2 and found that, when the other two factors are not the bottleneck, loss follows a **power law** in each of $N$, $D$ and $C$. The trends held across eight orders of magnitude in compute and six in model size. For model size the fit is:

blocks.caption: Kaplan et al. Eq. 1.1. N counts non-embedding parameters; models trained on enough data to not overfit.

blocks.md: Take logs of both sides: $\log L = \alpha_N \log N_c - \alpha_N \log N$. That is a straight line in $\log N$ with slope $-\alpha_N$. So on log-log axes a power law looks like a ruler-straight line, which is exactly what the paper's plots show. The exponent $\alpha_N$ is the whole story: it says how fast loss falls per multiplicative step in size.

blocks.title: Kaplan's L(N) with a movable model size

scenes.caption: At N = 10 million parameters the fit predicts a loss of 3.371 nats per token.
Ten times more parameters (100 million): loss 2.83. The loss was multiplied by 0.839.
1 billion: loss 2.376. Again multiplied by 0.839. Every 10x step gives the same ratio, which is why the curve is gently bent here but straight on log-log axes.
10 billion: loss 1.994. Drag the slider: the predicted gain per 10x never changes in ratio, but the absolute drop shrinks.

blocks.prompt: With $\alpha_N = 0.076$, doubling $N$ multiplies loss by $2^{-0.076}$. How many times larger must the model be to **halve** the loss, if this law kept holding?
blocks.reveal: About **9,100 times** larger, because $2^{1/0.076} \approx 9,139$. Doubling alone multiplies loss by only 0.949, about a 5% cut (the paper quotes 0.95). Small exponents mean huge multiplicative scale-ups for modest loss gains, which is why scaling is a compute story.

blocks.title: Same ratio per 10x, shrinking absolute gains

scenes.caption: Predicted loss at each size from the Kaplan fit. Each bar is the previous one times 0.839.
The absolute drops per 10x shrink: 0.541, 0.454, 0.381, 0.32. Constant ratio, diminishing absolute returns.

blocks.md: A pure power law heads to zero loss, which is impossible: text has irreducible randomness, so loss cannot fall below the entropy of the data. Kaplan et al. note the trend **must flatten out eventually**. Later fits (lesson 3) add a constant floor $E$. Also, loss values depend on the dataset and tokenizer, so numbers from different papers are not comparable.

A scaling law turns each multiplicative step in scale into a fixed **ratio** of loss. Fit the exponent on cheap runs, then extrapolate. Small exponents (around 0.05 to 0.1 here) mean big scale-ups buy modest gains.

blocks.question: A run at 100M non-embedding parameters reaches the loss Kaplan's fit predicts (2.83). Using the same law with ample data, what loss should a 10B model reach?
options: About 2.38
About 1.42, half the loss for 100x the size
About 1.99
About 2.83 minus 2 x 0.45, so 1.92
blocks.explain: Two 10x steps, each multiplying loss by 0.839: $2.83 \times 0.839^2 \approx 1.99$. 2.38 is only one step (1B). Subtracting a fixed amount per step assumes a linear trend, and halving would need about 9,139x more parameters, not 100x.

blocks.question: On log-log axes, a team's loss-versus-parameters points lie on a straight line with slope -0.07. Which statement is correct?
options: Each doubling of N removes the same fraction of the loss
Each doubling of N removes the same absolute amount of loss
Loss will reach zero at a finite model size
The slope says how much data the model needs
blocks.explain: A straight line in log-log space is a power law: equal multiplicative steps in N give equal multiplicative changes in L, here $2^{-0.07} \approx 0.95$ per doubling. Absolute drops shrink, the curve never reaches zero, and the slope says nothing about data needs on its own.

lessons.title: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND

blocks.md: A scaling law needs a common currency. The budget you actually have is **compute**: a number of floating point operations (FLOPs) you can afford. To compare a big model trained briefly with a small model trained long, you need to convert parameters and tokens into FLOPs.

Start with one token and a model with $N$ parameters. In the forward pass almost every parameter takes part in one multiply and one add for that token, so the forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs. The backward pass computes gradients for both activations and weights and costs about twice the forward pass, $4N$. Total: about $6N$ FLOPs per training token.

scenes.caption: One token flows through the network. Each parameter does roughly one multiply-add: about 2N FLOPs.
Backpropagation computes gradients with respect to activations and weights, roughly twice the forward cost: about 4N FLOPs.
Forward plus backward is about 6N FLOPs per token. Multiplying by D training tokens gives the run's compute.

blocks.caption: Kaplan et al. Sec. 2.1. It ignores the attention cost that grows with context length, which is small when d_model is large relative to context length / 12.

blocks.md: This approximation is what makes the three knobs trade off cleanly. For a fixed budget $C$, choosing $N$ fixes $D = C/(6N)$: a model twice as large can read only half as many tokens. Compute is often quoted in PF-days, where one PF-day is $10^{15} \times 86400 = 8.64 \times 10^{19}$ FLOPs.

blocks.title: From parameters and tokens to FLOPs and days
blocks.code:
N = 70e9            # parameters (Chinchilla)
D = 1.4e12          # training tokens
per_token = 6 * N   # 2N forward + 4N backward
C = per_token * D   # total training FLOPs
pf_days = C / 8.64e19          # 1 PF-day = 1e15 * 86400
gpus, flops_each = 1000, 4e14  # assumed sustained FLOP/s
days = C / (gpus * flops_each) / 86400
print(f'{C:.3g} FLOPs, {pf_days:.0f} PF-days, {days:.1f} days')

scenes.caption: Chinchilla's configuration: 70 billion parameters trained on 1.4 trillion tokens.
6N FLOPs per token.
Times D tokens gives the total training compute.
Converted to PF-days for comparison with the Kaplan paper's units.
Wall-clock depends on hardware and utilization. Simplified: we assume 1000 accelerators each sustaining 4e14 FLOP/s, an illustrative figure, not a measured one.

blocks.md: Apply the same arithmetic to real models. Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens) comes to 5.04e+23 FLOPs by 6ND; the Chinchilla paper reports 5.76e+23 using a more detailed count that includes attention and embeddings. Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) comes to 5.88e+23: the **same budget**, spent on a model 4 times smaller trained on about 4.7 times more tokens. Llama 3 405B on 15.6T tokens gives 3.79e+25, matching the 3.8e25 Meta reports.

blocks.title: Parameters, tokens and compute of four models

scenes.caption: Parameters in billions. Gopher is four times the size of Chinchilla.
Training tokens in billions. Chinchilla reads 1400B tokens, almost five times Gopher's 300B. LLaMA's smallest model reads 1000B.
Compute by 6ND in units of 1e21 FLOPs: 315, 504, 588, 40. Gopher and Chinchilla cost about the same; they just split it differently.

blocks.prompt: You double both the parameter count and the number of training tokens. By what factor does training compute grow?
blocks.reveal: **4x.** $C \approx 6ND$ is a product, so doubling both multiplies it by $2 \times 2$. This is why scaling both knobs together gets expensive fast, and why the question of how to split a budget between them matters so much.

blocks.md: 6ND counts useful model FLOPs, not wall-clock. Real hardware sustains only a fraction of its peak, so time and cost depend on utilization. And at long context lengths the attention term that 6N ignores stops being small. Serving a trained model costs about $2N$ FLOPs per generated token (forward pass only), which matters in lesson 5.
$C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

blocks.question: Your budget is fixed. You decide to make the model 3 times larger than planned. What must happen to the number of training tokens?
options: It stays the same, compute depends only on N
It must triple
It must drop to one third
It must drop to one ninth
blocks.explain: With $C \approx 6ND$ fixed, $D = C/(6N)$, so tripling N cuts D to one third. Compute depends on both knobs; nothing about the product is squared.

blocks.question: Using $C \approx 6ND$, roughly how much compute does a 405B-parameter model trained on 15.6T tokens use?
options: About 3.8e25 FLOPs
About 6.3e24 FLOPs
About 1.3e25 FLOPs
About 2.5e26 FLOPs
blocks.explain: $6 \times 4.05\times10^{11} \times 1.56\times10^{13} \approx 3.8e+25$ FLOPs, which matches the 3.8e25 Meta reports for Llama 3 405B. 6.3e24 forgets the factor 6; 1.3e25 uses 2N (inference cost) instead of 6N.

lessons.title: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves

blocks.md: Now the central question. You have a budget $C$. Every choice of $N$ fixes $D = C/(6N)$. Make the model too large and it sees too few tokens to learn what it can represent. Make it too small and it saturates: more tokens stop helping because it lacks capacity. Somewhere in between, loss is lowest. That model is **compute-optimal** for $C$.

Hoffmann et al. (2022), the Chinchilla paper, measured this directly. In their **IsoFLOP** approach they fixed 9 budgets from $6 \times 10^{18}$ to $3 \times 10^{21}$ FLOPs, trained models of many sizes at each budget (with the learning-rate schedule matched to each run's token count), and recorded the final loss. At each budget, loss against model size is a valley. They also fitted a single formula to all their runs:

blocks.caption: E: loss of an ideal model (entropy of the text). A/N^alpha: penalty for a finite model. B/D^beta: penalty for finite data and finite optimization.

blocks.md: Hoffmann et al. report $E = 1.69$, $A = 406.4$, $B = 410.7$, $\alpha = 0.34$, $\beta = 0.28$. In this lesson we plot the **refit by Besiroglu et al. (2024)**: $E = 1.8172$, $A = 482.01$, $B = 2085.43$, $\alpha = 0.3478$, $\beta = 0.3658$, fitted to data reconstructed from the Chinchilla paper. We use it because its optimum agrees with Chinchilla's other two methods; lesson 5 explains the disagreement. Simplified: losses are for DeepMind's MassiveText data; only the shape transfers.

blocks.title: Predicted loss over a grid of N and D (refit)

scenes.caption: Each cell is the refit loss for one (N, D) pair. Loss falls toward the bottom right, where both model and data are large.
The anti-diagonal cells all cost the same, 6ND = 6e22 FLOPs. Along it the loss goes 2.21, 2.11, 2.06, 2.05, 2.09, 2.17: a valley, lowest in the middle.
A 10x larger budget, 6e23 FLOPs: 2.01, 1.98, 1.97, 2.0. The valley moves down and to the right: both N and D grow.

blocks.title: IsoFLOP curve: loss vs model size at fixed compute

scenes.caption: C = 1e20 FLOPs. The valley bottoms out at N = 0.85B with D = 19.5B tokens, loss 2.553.
C = 1e21: optimum N = 2.78B, D = 60B, loss 2.306.
C = 1e22: N = 9.05B, D = 184B. Each 10x in compute moves the optimum N by about 3.3x.
Gopher's budget, 5.76e23: the refit's optimum is 72B parameters on 1.33T tokens, close to Chinchilla's 70B on 1.4T.

blocks.prompt: At Gopher's budget the optimum is about 72B parameters with loss 1.974. Which hurts more: a model 4x too **large** (and so 4x fewer tokens), or 4x too **small**?
blocks.reveal: Neither, much: both give about **1.994** (4x larger) and **1.994** (4x smaller), only 0.02 above the minimum. The valley is broad and nearly symmetric in log N. The Llama 3 team observed the same thing: IsoFLOP curves get flatter around the minimum as compute grows, so being somewhat off the optimal size costs little.

blocks.md: Because the formula is a sum of power laws, minimizing it under $C = 6ND$ has a closed form (Hoffmann et al., Eq. 4):

blocks.tex: N_{opt}(C) = G\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{a},\quad D_{opt}(C) = G^{-1}\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{b},\quad G = \left(\frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}},\ a = \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta},\ b = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}

blocks.md: With the refit, $a = 0.513$ and $b = 0.487$: parameters and tokens grow at almost the same rate, each roughly as $\sqrt{C}$. The resulting ratio is about 20 tokens per parameter (20.4 at 1e22 FLOPs, 18.4 at 5.76e23). Chinchilla's own table (Approach 1) says the same: 1B parameters wants 20.2B tokens, 10B wants 205.1B, 67B wants 1.5T.
Compute-optimal training scales model size and data **together**, each roughly as the square root of compute. The rule of thumb that falls out is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

Compute-optimal means lowest loss **per training FLOP**. It says nothing about the cost of serving the model afterwards, and the 20x ratio is tied to the data, architecture and training recipe it was measured on.

blocks.question: Under Chinchilla-style scaling (N and D each proportional to about $C^{0.5}$), your compute budget grows 10x. How should the model size change?
options: Grow about 10x, keeping tokens fixed
Grow about 5.4x
Grow about 3.2x, and tokens about 3.2x too
Stay fixed and train 10x longer
blocks.explain: $10^{0.5} \approx 3.16$ for both N and D, and $3.16 \times 3.16 = 10$ recovers the 10x compute. 5.4x is the Kaplan prescription ($10^{0.73}$) from the next lesson. Putting all of it into one knob walks up a wall of the IsoFLOP valley.

blocks.question: On an IsoFLOP curve, why does loss rise again for the largest models at a fixed budget?
options: Large models overfit any dataset
With compute fixed, a larger N leaves fewer tokens, so the data term B/D^beta grows
Large models have a larger irreducible loss E
Backward passes cost more than forward passes
blocks.explain: At fixed C, $D = C/(6N)$. Pushing N up shrinks D, and the finite-data penalty grows faster than the finite-model penalty falls. E is the same for every model, and the 6N cost is already accounted for in the budget.

lessons.title: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained

blocks.md: Kaplan et al. (2020) asked the same question and reached a different answer. Their fit said the optimal model size grows as $N \propto C^{0.73}$ while data grows only as $D \propto C^{0.27}$. Their summary: for a fixed budget you get the best loss by **training very large models and stopping significantly short of convergence**.

That advice shaped the large models that followed. Chinchilla's Table 1 lists GPT-3 (175B parameters, 300B tokens), Gopher (280B, 300B) and MT-NLG (530B, 270B): most large models of the time were trained on roughly 300B tokens regardless of size. Hoffmann et al. (2022) found instead that $N$ and $D$ should grow at about the same rate: exponents 0.50 and 0.50 (Approach 1), 0.49 and 0.51 (IsoFLOP), 0.46 and 0.54 (parametric fit).

blocks.title: How each law spends extra compute

scenes.caption: Kaplan's prescription: most extra compute goes into parameters. At 1000x compute, the model grows about 155x.
Under Kaplan, tokens grow only about 6.5x for that same 1000x, so tokens per parameter keep falling as models grow.
Chinchilla: both grow about 31.6x per 1000x compute, so the tokens-per-parameter ratio stays roughly constant.

blocks.prompt: Gopher used 5.76e23 FLOPs on 280B parameters and 300B tokens. Chinchilla's analysis said the optimal model for that budget is about 4x smaller on about 4x more tokens. What happened when they trained it?
blocks.reveal: Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens, same budget) **beat Gopher** across the board. On the MMLU benchmark (5-shot) it scored 67.6% against Gopher's 60.0%. It is also 4x cheaper to run per token, since inference cost scales with N.

scenes.caption: The Kaplan-era models: 0.51, 1.07 and 1.71 tokens per parameter.
Chinchilla: 1.4T tokens on 70B parameters, 20 tokens per parameter, the compute-optimal ratio.
Later models go further: Llama 3 405B at 38.5, and LLaMA's smallest model at about 149 (1T tokens on 6.7B). Lesson 5 explains why going past 20 can be deliberate.

blocks.md:
Why did Kaplan's fit point the wrong way? Three explanations, each from a paper that re-ran the analysis:

1. **Learning-rate schedule.** Kaplan used one schedule length for all runs and read losses off intermediate checkpoints. Hoffmann et al. showed a cosine schedule should be matched to the run's token count; mid-run checkpoints of a longer schedule show a higher loss than a properly scheduled short run reaches, which makes training on more tokens look less useful than it is.
2. **What counts as a parameter, and scale.** Pearce and Song (2024) found that counting only non-embedding parameters, combined with mostly small models, biases the fitted exponent toward Kaplan's value.
3. **Training details.** Porian et al. (2024) reproduced Kaplan's law, then removed it by accounting for last-layer compute, warmup length and scale-dependent optimizer tuning, which recovered Chinchilla's law. They also found careful learning-rate decay was *not* essential, contradicting explanation 1.

blocks.title: How the Kaplan exponent drifted to 0.73

scenes.caption: Kaplan et al. fitted the optimal-size exponent from their runs and got 0.73.
Pearce and Song: small scale plus non-embedding parameter counts bias the exponent upward.
Hoffmann et al. blamed the shared schedule; Porian et al. pointed to warmup, last-layer cost and optimizer tuning.
With those factors corrected, replications land near Chinchilla's 0.5 (Pearce and Song report 0.51).

blocks.md: Misconception: Kaplan's power laws were wrong. The loss-versus-size and loss-versus-data trends were real and still hold in shape. What shifted was the **compute-optimal allocation** derived from them, which is sensitive to experimental details. A scaling law is only as good as the runs it was fitted on.

blocks.question: GPT-3 used about 3.2e+23 FLOPs. Using $C \approx 6ND$ and Chinchilla's 20 tokens per parameter, what would a compute-optimal model at that budget look like?
options: 175B parameters on 300B tokens
About 500B parameters on 105B tokens
About 12B parameters on 4.3T tokens
About 51B parameters on 1.0T tokens
blocks.explain: Set $D = 20N$, so $C = 6 \cdot N \cdot 20N = 120N^2$ and $N = \sqrt{C/120} \approx 51$B, $D \approx 1.0$T. GPT-3's actual 175B on 300B tokens is the Kaplan-style choice; 12B on 4.3T overshoots the token ratio badly.

blocks.question: Which is the best summary of the Kaplan vs Chinchilla disagreement?
options: Chinchilla showed loss does not follow power laws
They agree that loss is a power law, but differ on how to split compute; replications trace Kaplan's split to experimental setup
Kaplan used more compute so its result is more reliable
The difference is only because they used different tokenizers
blocks.explain: Both papers find smooth power-law trends. The disagreement is the compute-optimal exponent (0.73 vs about 0.5), and later work explains it by schedule, parameter counting, small scale and optimizer details. Kaplan actually used smaller models than Chinchilla.

lessons.title: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break

blocks.md: Chinchilla minimizes **training** compute. But a deployed model is run for every token it serves, and a forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token. The LLaMA paper put it plainly: for a target level of performance, the preferred model is not the fastest to train but the fastest at inference. Its smallest model (6.7B parameters) was trained on 1T tokens, and the authors note a 7B model kept improving even after 1T tokens.

Sardana et al. (2024) made this precise. Fix the quality you need (a target loss $\ell$) and the number of tokens you expect to serve, $D_{inf}$. Then choose $N$ and training tokens $D_{tr}$ to minimize total lifetime compute:

A worked example with the refit from lesson 3. Target the loss of the compute-optimal model at Gopher's budget: 1.974. A smaller model can reach the same loss if it trains on more tokens. Solving $L(N, D) = 1.974$ for $D$: 72B needs 1.33T tokens, 50B needs 2.03T, 40B needs 2.81T, 30B needs 4.82T.

blocks.title: Lifetime compute for models of equal loss (units of 1e23 FLOPs)

scenes.caption: Training only. The compute-optimal 72B model is cheapest to train; 30B needs 1.51x the training compute for the same loss.
Add serving 10 trillion tokens at 2N FLOPs each. Now the 72B model is the most expensive in total, and 40B and 30B nearly tie for cheapest.
Serving 100 trillion tokens: inference dominates and the smallest model wins clearly, 68.68 vs 149.76.

blocks.prompt: Scanning all model sizes in this example, what is the cheapest choice when you expect to serve 10T tokens, and when you expect 100T?
blocks.reveal: At 10T served: about **34B parameters** on 3.7T tokens, about 109 tokens per parameter. At 100T served: about **21B** on 13.1T tokens, roughly 625 tokens per parameter. The more a model will be used, the further past 20 tokens per parameter it pays to train. This is called **overtraining** relative to Chinchilla.

blocks.md: Extreme ratios are extrapolations. Sardana et al. trained models up to 10,000 tokens per parameter and quality kept improving, but they also found that laws fitted at typical ratios **overestimate** the benefit of extra tokens at extreme ratios. Treat the hundreds-of-tokens-per-parameter numbers above as a direction, not a precise answer.

Real practice combines both ideas. For Llama 3, Meta ran scaling-law experiments from $6 \times 10^{18}$ to $10^{22}$ FLOPs with models from 40M to 16B parameters, fitted parabolas to each IsoFLOP curve and extrapolated to their 3.8e25 budget. The fit suggested 402B parameters on 16.55T tokens; they trained 405B on 15.6T. The smaller Llama 3 models were deliberately trained far longer than compute-optimal to be better at a fixed inference budget.

blocks.title: Llama 3: from small runs to a flagship forecast

nodes.label:
Power law: optimal
tokens vs compute

scenes.caption: Cheap runs at many sizes and budgets supply the data. Each IsoFLOP curve gets a parabola; its minimum is the compute-optimal model for that budget.
A power law through those minima, extrapolated about 3.5 orders of magnitude, sets the flagship's size and token count.
Loss is not accuracy, so a second chain maps compute to benchmark negative log-likelihood, then NLL to accuracy with a sigmoid. Meta reports it slightly underestimated the flagship's final score.

blocks.md: OpenAI reported something similar for GPT-4: a fit of the form $L(C) = aC^b + c$ to runs using at most 10,000x less compute predicted GPT-4's final loss with high accuracy. Scaling laws are now used as an engineering forecast before committing a large budget.

Where they break or mislead:

- **Loss is not ability.** Schaeffer et al. (2023) argue many reported **emergent abilities**, sudden jumps at some scale, come from nonlinear metrics like exact-match accuracy. With continuous metrics the same models improve smoothly.
- **Data runs out.** Muennighoff et al. (2023) found up to 4 epochs of repeated data is nearly as good as fresh data; beyond that the value of more compute decays toward zero.
- **Fits are fragile.** The rounded constants in the Chinchilla paper give an optimum at Gopher's budget of 32B parameters on 3.0T tokens by our calculation (93 tokens per parameter), inconsistent with the paper's other methods. Besiroglu et al. traced this to an optimizer that stopped early and rounding.

blocks.title: Optimal tokens per parameter: two fits of one formula

scenes.caption: The 20-to-1 rule from Chinchilla's Approaches 1 and 2, and the 70B on 1.4T model they trained.
Plugging the published, rounded Approach 3 constants into the closed form: the ratio climbs from about 32 to 153 across this range, contradicting the 20 they used.
The refit of the same formula stays near 20 (24 down to 16). Same functional form, different fitted constants, very different advice.

blocks.md: Chinchilla-optimal answers one question: lowest loss per training FLOP. Real decisions also weigh inference volume, available data and downstream metrics, so production models are often smaller and trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter.

blocks.question: A team will serve its model to millions of users for a year and needs a fixed quality bar. What does inference-aware scaling recommend?
options: Train the Chinchilla-optimal model, since it reaches the bar with the least compute
Train a smaller model on more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal, paying extra training compute to cut serving cost
Train the largest model the budget allows on fewer tokens, since bigger models are more sample-efficient
Train any size; inference cost does not depend on model size
blocks.explain: Serving costs about 2N FLOPs per token, so with heavy usage a smaller model that reaches the same loss by training longer has lower lifetime cost. Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute only. Bigger-and-shorter is Kaplan's advice and makes serving more expensive.

blocks.question: Exact-match accuracy on a task jumps from near 0% to 60% between two model sizes, while per-token loss falls smoothly. What is the most careful reading?
options: The larger model suddenly acquired a new capability that scaling laws cannot describe
The metric is nonlinear: smooth per-token gains compound into an all-or-nothing score, so the jump may be partly a metric effect
The loss measurement must be wrong
The smaller model was undertrained, which fully explains the jump
blocks.explain: Schaeffer et al. show that discontinuous metrics like exact match can turn smooth improvement into apparent jumps, and continuous metrics make the trend smooth again. That is why Llama 3 forecast accuracy through NLL first. It does not prove no real change ever happens, but the jump alone is not evidence of one.
